The structural hierarchy of patent types—primary, secondary, and derivative—mirrors a mathematical lattice where each level represents a distinct layer of intellectual property inheritance. Primary inventions define foundational types with broad scope, while secondary patents depend on prior rights and are thus subordinate. Deviations from these types introduce ambiguity, modeled through fuzzy boundaries. The interplay between these layers generates a dualistic logic: one of legal certainty and one of contested interpretation. Each invention type maps to a probabilistic belief structure in GSI, where Bayesian updating reflects evolving legal consensus. In GSE, this manifests as state transitions within an innovation graph, where agents navigate the space of allowable modifications. Failure modes arise when boundary conditions are violated, leading to legal disputes or invalidation of claims. This framework supports both formal reasoning about invention validity and dynamic simulation of innovation pathways.
